surfaces.part: asphalt road network patches (crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends) on dirt/gravel ground

answer.evidence: The image is a flat, seamless ground tile seen straight down: gray-brown gravel and dirt with teal-gray asphalt strips forming crossroads, T-junctions and dead ends. There is no standing volume, no front (south) face and no roof or lid ellipse. The dark ragged lines under the road edges are crack or edge shading, not an eave. For terrain this is the expected flat top-down drawing, so it reads as a top-down slab with no front face rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 8 visible tones per 16x16 tile, against 3 for the grass reference and 7 for the paving reference. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references, so there are no flat fills. The dirt field carries scattered speckle, pebble dots and rust and brown patches in about 4-5 steps. The asphalt strips have a dark slate edge, a mid body, and lighter chips and cracks along the broken borders. The 0% near-neutral share of dark edge pixels means the dark edges lean toward the material's own colour, not neutral black, so it does not read as a sticker outline. The weaknesses are that the asphalt body is fairly uniform with sparse crack detail, and the whole piece uses only 13 colours, so its ramps are slightly shallower than Beodeul's 5-6 steps. Even so, it is not flatter than the references on the measured facts or by eye, and the ground reads as textured.
